_podcast.theme_scoring_prompt:
Rate how well this article fits the theme 'Indigenous Lands & Innovation' — Indigenous nations using technology, governance, and stewardship on their own terms.

OUT OF SCOPE — score 0-9: geopolitical and war news with no Indigenous rights angle; general wildfire and wildlife-service updates not led by or directly affecting Indigenous communities or guardians; provincial forestry and environmental policy with no explicit First Nations involvement; consumer tech and gadget reviews; science with no Indigenous stewardship or sovereignty context; crime and judicial news unrelated to Indigenous rights.

CALIBRATION — apply this ladder to everything else. Indigenous-led journalism on governance, rights, and self-determination is a strong fit on its own: a technology hook raises a score but is NOT required to reach the top band.
- 80-100: Excellent Indigenous-led reporting. Cariboo stories bridging governance or culture AND technology land here (Tŝilhqot'in/Secwépemc/Dakelh language revitalization tech, guardian programs using sensors and drones, GIS land mapping, Indigenous-led connectivity, digital heritage projects) — and so does outstanding national coverage of sovereignty, treaty, and land rights.
- 55-79: Solid pan-Canadian Indigenous governance, sovereignty, land rights, treaty, or reconciliation journalism — APTN, Eagle Feather News, or IndigiNews-style coverage of First Nations governance, MMIWG, land claims, self-determination, and Indigenous-led services. Most Indigenous governance journalism belongs HERE, not below.
- 30-54: Indigenous cultural, community, or human-interest stories (awards, events, ceremonies) with limited governance substance, or BC land-stewardship and environmental stories with meaningful First Nations involvement.
- 10-29: General BC land, environmental, or forestry stories that mention Indigenous communities only in passing.

ANCHORS: 'Tŝilhqot'in Nation launches drone-based caribou monitoring on title lands' → 98. 'First Nations leaders reject BC's revised land-title framework' → 75. 'Secwépemc language app reaches 1,000 learners' → 88. 'BC Wildfire Service updates evacuation alerts for the Interior' → 8.

Score 0-100 where 100 is a perfect thematic match and 0 is completely unrelated.

items.title: [The Guardian Global Development] Curse of the Nile’s gold: how Sudan is losing its fertile fields and ability to produce food
items.content_html:
🪶 ✏️

An artisanal mining boom driven by war and poverty is causing a public health emergency, as chemicals poison soil, water and society

In Abu Hamad, on the banks of the Nile, verdant orchards, gardens and fields once produced a bounty of dates, citrus fruits, winter grains and cereals for the towns and cities of eastern Sudan, including Khartoum and Port Sudan.

Today, the land looks drastically different. Trees have been cut down, agricultural areas cleared, and farms have been replaced by shops and commercial sites. Dotted around the town and its outskirts, more than 700 mounds of grey waste are poisoning the soil, water and air. The mounds are the toxic remnants of artisanal gold mining, a practice that began in about 2008 and has intensified over the past six years.

Continue reading...

items.title: [Fast Company] Thousands of security workers for Big Tech companies are on strike in California
items.content_html:
🪶 ✏️

Security officers at some of the most prominent tech companies in Silicon Valley have been poised to walk off the job since voting to authorize a strike earlier this month. The workers have been in talks with major security contractors like Securitas and Allied Universal for months as they seek to reach a new contract agreement.

Now, as contract negotiations have stalled, 14,000 security officers represented by SEIU-United Service Workers West are striking across California. The union members took to the streets in San Francisco and Los Angeles at 4:30 a.m. local time on Friday to push for meaningful wage increases and better benefits. 

The SEIU-USWW campaign has highlighted the gulf between hourly pay for security workers and the deep coffers of the tech giants who use their services. While the workers are technically employed by third-party contractors, the union has said they provide building security for companies like OpenAI, Anthropic, Salesforce, Google, Amazon, Microsoft, Meta, Nvidia, Cisco, and Netflix; they also serve a variety of other employers, from hospitals to retailers. 

According to the union, some of the security contractors have proposed a mere $0.65 raise in hourly pay over the next two years; Allied Universal, the largest security firm in the world, reportedly offered a wage increase of just $0.25 per hour in 2027, with no raises for the following three years.

SEIU-USWW president David Huerta previously described this proposal as “shameful, wrong, and deeply, deeply disrespectful.” 

In a statement, an Allied Universal spokesperson said: “We have made substantial progress in negotiations as part of our commitment to finding common ground. We value the ongoing dialogue, have approached discussions with flexibility and a willingness to work collaboratively toward solutions, and remain focused on reaching a fair and mutually beneficial agreement.” (Securitas was not immediately available for comment.)

Security personnel have become even more critical as companies like OpenAI and Anthropic have faced threats amid mounting public distrust of AI. A few weeks ago, Business Insider reported that Anthropic had instructed its employees to work from home, in case their security officers decided to go on strike.

“Clearly, Anthropic understands how indispensable security workers are, even if the companies bargaining with them don’t,” Huerta told Bay Area public media outlet KQED recently. 

In the meantime, median pay for security workers in California remains around $20 per hour, according to an analysis by the UC Berkeley Labor Center. While median pay for security officers is higher in the Bay Area—closer to $24 per hour—that’s still significantly lower than the median wage for all workers in the region, which crosses $42 per hour.

In Los Angeles, median pay for security workers is less than $20 per hour, a figure noticeably lower than the median wage for all workers in the greater L.A. area, which is higher than $27 per hour.

According to the UC Berkeley analysis, more than 44% of all security officers in California qualify as low-wage workers; in the Bay Area, more than two-thirds of security workers are classified as low-wage. 

The SEIU-USWW members who went on strike Friday are aiming for hourly pay of $30, along with more affordable healthcare coverage, expanded retirement benefits, and robust training. Contract workers who provide ancillary services to tech companies have previously walked off the job, often ramping up public pressure on those employers to negotiate more favorable terms with third-party contractors. 

In its recent demonstrations, the union has pointed out that as the cost of living continues to rise precipitously in cities like San Francisco, security workers may eventually have no choice but to leave if their pay doesn’t improve—to the detriment of the many companies that have come to rely on their labor.

items.title: [Pinterest Engineering Blog - Medium] Evolving Pinterest’s Embedding Retrieval Platform
items.content_html:
🪶 ✏️

Authors: Bowen Zhou | Staff Software Engineer; Shan Gao | Senior Software Engineer; Jingwen Hu | Software Engineer II; Wenjiang Chu | Staff Software Engineer

The Billion-Embedding Challenge

At Pinterest, the “signal” is our lifeblood. Whether it’s a home decor enthusiast finding the perfect rug or a fashion seeker discovering a new aesthetic, our discovery engine relies on understanding deep semantic relationships to help our users find inspirations. Over the last few years, the explosive growth of embedding-based retrieval has fundamentally transformed how we surface these signals — and at the heart of that transformation is Manas, Pinterest’s in-house distributed search platform.

Embedding Retrieval is one of the core capabilities of Manas, supporting multiple approximate nearest neighbor search algorithms, hybrid queries with both token and embedding clauses, as well as real-time updates to ensure fresh contents become searchable within seconds. Deployed on over 80 clusters and serving billions of embeddings, Manas embedding retrieval powers all major product surfaces at Pinterest including Home Feed, Search, Related Pins, Ads, and Notifications.

However, as our corpus scales toward tens of billions of embeddings and our models capture increasingly complex interactions, we face mounting challenges around cost efficiency, scalability, and flexibility. On the infrastructure side, traditional ANN algorithms like HNSW are notoriously memory-hungry — they require the entire index to reside in RAM to maintain low query latency, making cost grow linearly with corpus size. On the modeling side, the classic two-tower retrieval paradigm is too restrictive: it reduces each candidate to a single embedding and scores relevance through a simple dot product, leaving little room to express richer, context-dependent notions of similarity.

To tackle these challenges, our team has been evolving Manas’s embedding retrieval stack across three fronts:

  • Quantization. We reduce the memory footprint of embedding indices by compressing vectors into lower-bit representations with fewer effective dimensions. Quantization has been rolled out to all major use cases, delivering over 50% memory reduction in embedding indices and 20–30% cost savings in serving infrastructure.
  • SSD-based Serving. Rather than holding entire indices in RAM, we serve ANN queries directly from SSD by carefully bounding the I/O per request — sustaining high throughput with low tail latencies at a fraction of the memory cost. Early experiments demonstrate a 10x reduction in memory usage and 40% CPU savings compared to in-memory serving
  • Multi-embedding Retrieval. We move beyond the single-vector-per-candidate constraint of the two-tower model by supporting richer scoring functions that consider multiple embeddings per candidate. This unlocks more expressive ranking at the retrieval stage. We are currently partnering with a product team to launch a pilot use case.

In this blog post, we will delve into the technical details and results of each initiative, and discuss what’s next for embedding retrieval in Manas.

Quantization: Redefining the Footprint of High-Recall Search

For a long time, serving embeddings in 16-bit or 32-bit float precision was considered the common practice. But at Pinterest’s scale, raw precision is a luxury that often provides diminishing returns. We discovered that quantization — transforming these high-dimensional float vectors into compact integer representations — is one of our most effective ways to better cost efficiency.

Evaluating the Trade-offs: SQ vs. PQ

In the Manas stack, we focused our implementation on two primary quantization algorithms: Scalar Quantization (SQ) and Product Quantization (PQ). The core of these methodologies lies in partitioning the vector space into disjoint subspaces and mapping each vector into an integer representation: SQ applies uniform discretization from float to integer per dimension, while PQ performs a K-Means clustering in each subspace and maps a subvector to the ID of the closest cluster centroid.

Benchmarks on a 100-million-embedding GraphSage dataset confirmed this intuition. We evaluated both SQ and PQ across two ANN algorithms (HNSW and IVF) and observed a clear trade-off: PQ achieves higher compression but with a significant recall decrease, while SQ delivers strong compression with minimal loss on recall.

  • PQ reduces the HNSW index by 74% and the IVF index by 93%, with a recall in the range of 70–80%
  • SQ reduces the HNSW index by 59% and the IVF index by 75%, with a recall over 90% consistently

Given the trade-off demonstrated by the offline benchmarking exercise, we ran online A/B experiments in production to select the best performing quantizer for each use case, and ensure negligible impact on user engagement metrics when enabling quantization. We launched SQ and PQ across major product use cases, reducing the total memory allocation significantly and realizing 20–30% cost savings for serving.

Technical Deep Dive: SIMD and Linear Scaling

Shifting to 8-bit or 4-bit representations isn’t just a memory win; it’s a compute challenge. Usually, SQ requires a decoding step before distance computation, which can become a CPU bottleneck. To solve this, we implemented Linear Scaling SQ, which quantizes a vector by scaling only, and thus eliminates the decoding step before distance computation. The key enabler here is SIMD intrinsics, which allows the CPU to perform multiple 8-bit integer operations with each instruction, and hence reduces the total computing resources needed per query by 10–15% in our use cases.

SSD Serving: Moving Beyond the Constraints of RAM

Our journey of improving embedding retrieval cost efficiency led us to exploring alternative ANN algorithms that take advantage of recent NVMe SSD performance advancements. The current generation of SSD devices are roughly an order of magnitude cheaper per gigabyte, but with the latency increased from nanoseconds to microseconds, which can slow down queries if I/O operations are not carefully managed. To bridge this gap, we experimented with I/O-aware ANN algorithms that were designed to minimize the number of random reads issued per query while retaining a recall score as good as memory-based algorithms.

DiskANN vs. SPANN

In our experiments, we benchmarked two disk-based ANN algorithms, DiskANN and SPANN, with a 100M-embedding corpus collected from a Pinterest Search use case. While DiskANN is a robust graph-based approach, SPANN emerged as the better option for the Manas use cases.

Our team’s key observation was applying PQ quantization to the on-disk embedding store while retaining the full precision centroids helped the search accuracy and throughput significantly — a slight tweak from the original SPANN paper. This makes SPANN+PQ 4.5x faster than plain SPANN and achieves over 3x the QPS of DiskANN with 1/3 the latency, with a slight 5% recall drop.

Implementing SPANN in Manas

We implemented the SPANN algorithm in Manas, which stores the centroid index in the memory and the large posting lists in the disk, and guarantees both disk-access efficiency (low latency) and high recall by effectively reducing the disk access number per request. In the index-building stage, we adopt the hierarchical balanced clustering algorithm from SPANN for selecting the centroids, which ensures evenly distributed cluster sizes, and hence similar lengths of posting lists to keep the tail latency low. We build the centroid index using HNSW, which is well-suited for in-memory search over a relatively small set of centroids. In a preliminary evaluation with a Pin recommendation use case that indexes over 5 billion embeddings, our SPANN implementation saves over 40% of CPU time for production queries when compared with HNSW, with a <5% recall drop. Our next step is to adopt SPANN across all major use cases.

Multi-Embedding Retrieval: The Shift Toward Late Interaction

As we improve cost efficiency, we are also evolving the expressivity of the Manas embedding retrieval stack. The traditional “Two-Tower” model, while efficient, collapses an entire Pin or query into a single vector, often losing the nuanced, token-level semantics that define high-quality discovery.

Contrast in Paradigms: Sum of MaxSim

We are now moving toward Late Interaction models , such as ColBERT. Unlike the single dot product of two-tower models, late interaction represents documents and queries as lists of vectors. We use the “Sum of MaxSim” scoring logic to capture the maximum similarity between each query token and the document’s tokens.

Integrating this into Manas required comprehensive changes in our serving stack. We integrated the multi-embedding retrieval as a new query type and updated Manas to handle multiple query embeddings rather than a single vector per query. This required updating the Manas query parser to understand these complex queries, as well as running multiple ANN searches from a multi-embedding query simultaneously. Currently, we are working with a client team to launch a pilot use case for the multi-embedding query support in Manas. This represents the next frontier of Pinterest search: moving from “two tower” to true model-based retrieval.

Looking Ahead

The future of vector search at Pinterest lies at the intersection of infrastructure efficiency and retrieval model innovation. Over the next five years, our central goal is to evolve Manas embedding retrieval into an architecture that is scalable, cost-efficient, and open to new retrieval paradigms. We are pursuing this along three directions: adopting SPANN and SPFresh to push CPU and memory costs even lower for billion-scale indices; building first-class support for multi-embedding retrieval models like ColBERT that enable richer, interaction-based scoring at the retrieval stage; and embracing GPU-based retrieval systems like SilverTorch and TIGER to unlock new model capabilities.

Special thanks to Ellie Madsen, Jennifer Kong, and Jiawei Kuang for working on various Manas embedding retrieval projects. items.title: [Fast Company] We know how to shape systems to better support working mothers. So why don’t we?
items.content_html:
🪶 ✏️

As more women join the workforce and gradually gain representation in leadership roles, the lack of resources like affordable childcare and paid maternity leave has become increasingly consequential. 

In the first half of last year, the U.S. saw the steepest decline of working mothers with children under 5 years old in 40 years, according to a University of Kansas study, and that decline has continued.

During this week’s Fast Company Innovation Festival, staff editor Shalene Gupta asked several mothers in senior leadership positions how we got here, what mothers need, and how we can improve workplaces and support systems accordingly.

We’ve been here before

Panelists noted that governments and workplaces have already shown that they can adapt.

Girls Who Code founder Reshma Saujani, now CEO of Moms First—an organization that advocates for paid leave and affordable childcare—said that during World War II, the Lanham Act created the country’s first national childcare program, supporting many of the millions of women who suddenly entered the workforce.

“The minute men came back to work, so what did we do? We dismantled all those childcare centers,” she said.

At the onset of the COVID-19 pandemic, women lost 1.5 million more jobs than men, according to Indeed’s Hiring Lab; even so, it was a time in which workplaces offered more flexibility for parents, and billions in government childcare funding helped more women enter or remain in the workforce. 

Then, those systems were shut down, too, Saujani said. 

Affordable childcare is a broadly popular concept

Families have made it clear that affordable childcare is a priority, she said, referencing New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani’s emphasis on providing no-cost childcare. 

Another thing we learned during the pandemic, and are now seeing in response to AI, is “that companies can get really nimble, really quick” when growth and capital are on the line, said Alison Moore, CEO of Chief, a private membership network for women in leadership. 

Moore said we need to apply that same mindset to human capital—and the changes we’ve seen so far haven’t been enough.

Outside of the workplace, there are other gaps in available support for mothers, especially new mothers, said Latham Thomas, CEO and founder of the doula-training company Mama Glow and the nonprofit Mama Glow Foundation.

Doulas, for example, provide emotional and physical support and education, she said; but they also work to “ensure that there are systems in place when your baby arrives, so that when they leave, you can actually function.”

They look for gaps in care, Thomas said, and unfortunately, current systems in the U.S. often mean paying people to fill those gaps. The people in those caregiving professions aren’t well taken care of either, she said. 

“They’re underinsured, they’re under-resourced, they’re underpaid,” Thomas added. “And quite frankly, those are the people that we need to be shoring up the most support for financially, and building institutional frameworks for, to ensure that they can be a part of our journey as we advance as women.”

Saujani added that we already know what to do. “The question you’ve got to ask yourself is, why don’t we do it?”

The impossibility of being a working mother in America is due to intentional policy failures, Saujani said. “And every time we get close to fixing these structural failures, we get handed a culture war”—like the false choice between being a tradwife or a girlboss. 

Until we get past those divisions, she said, we can’t fix things to “finally build a country that works for mothers.”
